title: Design an S3-like Object Storage System
prompt: Design an S3-like object storage system: clients PUT and GET arbitrary blobs (bytes to terabytes) under bucket/key names, with very high durability and availability. Cover how you store the bytes, track metadata, and achieve durability cost-effectively.
blurb: The durable-blob-at-scale problem — separating metadata from data, chunking large objects, and replication vs erasure coding for eleven-nines durability.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (PUT/GET/DELETE, list, multipart, versioning) from non-functional (durability e.g. 11 nines, availability, throughput for large objects, cost).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks about object size distribution, read/write ratio, durability/availability targets, consistency model, throughput vs latency priorities.

rubric.label: Back-of-envelope estimations
rubric.description: Derives capacity/year, object count and metadata size, network throughput, and node/disk counts.

rubric.label: Metadata / data separation
rubric.description: A metadata service (bucket/key -> chunk locations) separate from the data plane (chunk/blob stores); why coupling them limits scale.

rubric.label: Chunking & large objects
rubric.description: Splitting large objects into fixed chunks, multipart upload, parallelism, resumability, and how chunk placement is tracked.

rubric.label: Durability: replication vs erasure coding
rubric.description: Replication (simple, 3x storage) vs erasure coding (e.g. 10+4, ~1.4x, cheaper, higher repair/latency cost); reasoning about failure domains.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Client -> LB/API -> metadata service + data placement -> chunk servers -> background repair/scrubbing; read/write paths.

rubric.label: Consistency model
rubric.description: Read-after-write for new objects, overwrite/versioning semantics, eventual list consistency, atomic commit of a multipart upload.

rubric.label: Scaling
rubric.description: Sharding metadata, spreading chunks across failure domains, rebalancing on node add/loss, hot-object handling / caching / CDN.

rubric.label: Reliability & repair
rubric.description: Detecting silent corruption (scrubbing, checksums), re-replication / re-encoding on disk loss, bounding repair traffic.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Durability accounting, under-replicated object counts, repair backlog, request latency/error SLOs, capacity headroom.

functional_requirements: PUT / GET / DELETE an object by bucket + key
List objects in a bucket (by prefix)
nonfunctional_requirements: High availability for reads and writes
High throughput for large objects; reasonable small-object latency
clarifying_questions: Object size distribution — mostly small, or many multi-GB blobs?
Read/write ratio and throughput vs latency priorities?
Consistency model — strong read-after-write, or eventual?
Do we need versioning, lifecycle/tiering, and encryption at rest?
qualifying_questions: Is storage cost or write latency the harder constraint?
Are objects mostly immutable (write-once) or frequently overwritten?
What are the failure domains — disk, node, rack, AZ?

estimations.capacity: 1B objects/day avg 1MB = ~1PB/day ingest; a year is hundreds of PB — plan for continuous fleet growth.
estimations.metadata: Object metadata ~1KB each; 100B objects -> ~100TB of metadata -> must be a sharded, indexed store, not a single DB.
estimations.durability_math: 3x replication survives 2 concurrent losses per object; 10+4 erasure coding survives any 4 of 14 shards at ~1.4x overhead vs 3x — big cost win at large scale.
estimations.throughput: Multi-GB objects demand parallel chunk transfer; a single object saturates many disks/NICs at once.

data_model: objects(bucket_id, key, version_id, size, etag, chunk_list, created_at)
api_design: PUT /{bucket}/{key} (body) -> etag; large uploads via multipart
POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploads (init) + PUT part + POST complete -> atomic commit
reference.high_level_design: The gateway authenticates and routes to the metadata service, which maps bucket/key to an ordered chunk list. On PUT, the object is split into fixed-size chunks; each chunk is either replicated N ways or erasure-coded into k+m shards, and the placement service spreads those shards across distinct failure domains (disk/node/rack/AZ). Chunk servers store shards with checksums; the metadata commit that records the chunk map is the atomic 'the object now exists' point (enabling read-after-write). On GET, metadata yields the chunk list and the data plane streams/reassembles (decoding erasure shards if needed). A background scrubber verifies checksums and a repair service re-replicates or re-encodes chunks when disks/nodes are lost, bounded to avoid saturating the network. A GC reclaims space from deleted/overwritten versions.

deep_dives.probe: Replication vs erasure coding — walk through the storage overhead and failure tolerance of 3x replication vs a 10+4 code, and when you'd pick each. How do read latency and repair cost differ?
How do you handle a 5TB multipart upload — chunk size, parallelism, resumability, and how the final 'complete' becomes atomic and consistent?
How do you place shards so no single rack/AZ failure can lose an object, and how do you rebalance when you add capacity or lose a node?
How do you provide read-after-write for a new object, and what are the semantics for overwrite, versioning, and list-after-delete?
A disk holding thousands of shards dies. How do you detect it, re-encode/re-replicate the affected chunks, and keep repair traffic from overwhelming the cluster?

Your metadata store is the system of record for object locations. How do you feed downstream consumers — bucket indexing/listing, lifecycle rules, analytics — off metadata changes? Change data capture / Debezium, or emitting events on commit?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions erasure or reed-solomon or coding
followup_bank.question: What k+m parameters, and how does that change read latency (must fetch k shards) and repair bandwidth vs plain replication?
What is the cache eviction policy for hot objects, and how do you avoid a stampede when a viral object's cache entry expires and thousands of GETs hit the data plane at once?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions metadata or database or postgres or sql or dynamo
followup_bank.question: How is the metadata store sharded, and how do you stream metadata changes to listing/lifecycle/analytics consumers — CDC/Debezium vs dual writes?
What chunk size do you pick and why, and how is the multipart 'complete' made atomic so a partial upload is never readable?
Across how many failure domains do you spread replicas, and what durability do 3 copies actually buy vs an erasure code at the same cost?

scaling: Shard metadata by bucket/key hash; keep it separate from the data plane
Spread chunk shards across disks/racks/AZs; rebalance on capacity change
Parallelize large-object transfer across many chunk servers
Tier cold data to cheaper media; cache/CDN hot objects
Bound and prioritize repair traffic to protect foreground I/O
bottlenecks: Metadata service hotspots for hot buckets/prefixes
Repair bandwidth after large disk/node loss
Hot-object read amplification without a cache/CDN
tradeoffs: Replication (simple, fast reads, 3x cost) vs erasure coding (~1.4x cost, slower reads/repair)
Larger chunks (less metadata, coarse repair) vs smaller chunks (fine repair, more metadata)
Aggressive repair (fast recovery, I/O contention) vs throttled (safe, longer under-replication window)
alternative_solutions: Full 3x replication only (simpler, higher cost) for latency-sensitive tiers
Erasure coding for cold/bulk tiers, replication for hot
Log-structured storage with GC (append-only chunk files)
LSM/HDFS-style with a single metadata master (simpler, master scaling limits)
observability: Request latency/error SLOs by size class
security: Per-bucket/object access policies and signed URLs
Encryption at rest (per-object keys) and in transit
Authn/authz on every request; tenant isolation
Audit logging of access and admin actions
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer separates a sharded metadata service (bucket/key -> chunk map) from a data plane of chunk servers, chunks large objects for parallel/resumable multipart uploads, and chooses durability deliberately: replication for hot/latency-sensitive data and erasure coding (e.g. 10+4, ~1.4x) for bulk, spreading shards across failure domains. The metadata commit is the atomic point giving read-after-write. It runs a checksum scrubber and a throttled repair/re-encode loop on disk loss, plans rebalancing and hot-object caching/CDN, and streams metadata changes (CDC) to listing/lifecycle/analytics. It names metadata hotspots and repair bandwidth as the key bottlenecks.

interviewer_notes: The signal is in three places: separating metadata from the data plane, chunking large objects (multipart, atomic complete), and reasoning quantitatively about durability — replication vs erasure coding overhead and failure domains. Do not accept 'store 3 copies' without asking about cost at scale and whether erasure coding fits. If they place a metadata store, hit the CDC/Debezium probe; if they add a hot-object cache/CDN, probe eviction and stampede. Push on the repair story after a disk dies (detection, re-encode, bounded bandwidth) and on consistency semantics for overwrite/versioning/list.
